scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is asking whether refusing to pump their girlfriend's tire is morally acceptable. The question is to evaluate if the action is morally acceptable (1) or not (0), and respond only in the specified format.

First, I need to understand the scenario properly. The person (let's call them the boyfriend) has been dealing with his girlfriend expecting him to handle car maintenance issues, especially tire problems. He noticed a low tire, told her, then when it went flat, he fixed it. He bought her a PSI gauge and taught her how to use it. But she keeps asking him to do things beyond his expertise, like checking pressure daily and taking it to the gas station. He's made it clear he doesn't know much about car repairs beyond basics, but she insists he should learn or ask her dad. He offered to show her again, but she refused, saying it's a man's responsibility and that her male friends/family agree. He points out he does housework, cooks, pays most expenses, and doesn't hold her to gender stereotypes, but she does to him.

Now, the key question: is refusing to pump the tire morally acceptable?

Moral acceptability here depends on principles like mutual respect, shared responsibilities, and not enforcing outdated gender roles. The boyfriend has already taught her how to do it, provided tools, and made it clear he's not a mechanic. She's insisting he do it because of gender roles, which he's rejecting. He's not refusing out of laziness but because he's been clear about his limits and she's not taking responsibility herself.

In a healthy relationship, responsibilities should be shared based on ability and willingness, not gender. If she's refusing to learn despite being taught, and insisting on gender-based expectations, then his refusal to comply with unreasonable demands is reasonable. He's not being unhelpful; he's setting boundaries. He's done his part by teaching her and providing tools. Her insistence on him doing it because she's "helpless" and it's a "man's responsibility" is problematic. So refusing to do it when she's not willing to learn herself is morally acceptable.

But wait, is there a moral obligation to help? Well, in a relationship, helping each other is good, but it shouldn't be one-sided. If she's not taking responsibility for her own car maintenance despite being taught, then he's not obligated to keep doing it. Especially since she's using gender stereotypes to justify it, which he's rejecting. His refusal is about setting boundaries against unfair expectations.

Also, the fact that he pays most expenses and does housework shows he's contributing, but she's expecting him to handle car stuff because he's male. That's not fair. So refusing to do it when she's not willing to learn is morally acceptable.

So the answer should be 1. The action is morally acceptable.

Check if there's any angle where it's not. Maybe if the car is shared or something, but the scenario says "her car," so it's her responsibility. He's not her mechanic. She's the owner, so she should maintain it. He's helped before, but she's not taking initiative. So yes, refusing is okay.

Yes, answer 1.
